name: Basque (Euskara)

sandhi_rules.name: ez+d→ezt (regressive devoicing)
sandhi_rules.notes: ez + d- → ezt-: the voiced /d/ of the following word devoices to [t] after the laminal sibilant of ez while the sibilant is retained — ez dut → eztut [es̻ tut], ez da → ezta [es̻ ta], ez dakit → eztakit [es̻ takit]. Categorical connected-speech sandhi of the negative particle ez /es̻/ before a following auxiliary/verb-initial consonant, obligatory for all speakers of Standard Basque and pan-Basque across the dialects (the DEGREE/spelling of the assimilation varies dialectally, but the contractions themselves are general): Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003, Hualde 'Segmental phonology' §2 (consonant assimilation / sandhi of the negative particle), pp.15-65; Hualde 1991, Basque Phonology, §on the negative particle ez. Modelled on eu (Batua) and inherited by the historical-dialect specs via the id-keyed sandhi overlay; a dialect that does not realise ez as /es̻/ simply does not fire the rule (null beats a wrong contraction).

sandhi_rules.name: ez+z→etz (sibilant→affricate coalescence)
sandhi_rules.notes: ez + z- → etz-: the sibilant of ez coalesces with the following laminal sibilant into the laminal affricate [ts̻], leaving the vowel of ez bare — ez zen → etzen [e ts̻en], ez zara → etzara [e ts̻aɾa]. Categorical connected-speech sandhi of the negative particle ez /es̻/ before a following auxiliary/verb-initial consonant, obligatory for all speakers of Standard Basque and pan-Basque across the dialects (the DEGREE/spelling of the assimilation varies dialectally, but the contractions themselves are general): Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003, Hualde 'Segmental phonology' §2 (consonant assimilation / sandhi of the negative particle), pp.15-65; Hualde 1991, Basque Phonology, §on the negative particle ez. sandhi_rules.name: ez+n→en (sibilant deletion before nasal)
sandhi_rules.notes: ez + n- → en-: the sibilant of ez is deleted before a following nasal — ez naiz → enaiz [e nais̻], ez nator → enator [e natoɾ]. notes: Standard Basque (Euskara Batua), codified by the Royal Academy of the Basque Language (Euskaltzaindia) from 1968. Conservative Basque varieties have a three-way sibilant place contrast: lamino-alveolar /s̻/ (spelled z), apico-alveolar /s̺/ (spelled s) and postalveolar /ʃ/ (spelled x), with the matching affricates /ts̻/ (tz), /ts̺/ (ts) and /tʃ/ (tx); this three-way contrast is fully stable in eastern and Navarrese varieties such as Goizueta but is neutralised further west (Hualde, Lujanbio & Zubiri 2010: 119). Palatal stops /c/ (tt) and /ɟ/ (dd), palatal nasal /ɲ/ (ñ) and palatal lateral /ʎ/ (ll) arise historically by palatalisation of /t d n l/ after /i/. Voiced stops /b d ɡ/ are realised as approximants [β ð ɣ] intervocalically (Hualde et al. 2010: 116), and nasals assimilate in place to a following consonant (2010: 120). Five vowels /i e a o u/. Aspiration (/h/, aspirated stops) is preserved only in the eastern (continental) dialects and was lost in the west (Hualde 2018: 2). Dialectal variation across the historical dialects is extensive; Batua draws primarily from Gipuzkoan and Lapurdian sources. Basque is a language isolate with no demonstrated genetic relationship to any other language family. Single ⟨r⟩ is a tap [ɾ] in the onset — intervocalically and in obstruent+r clusters (⟨tr pr kr gr br dr fr⟩) — but the tap/trill contrast is neutralised in the syllable coda, where it surfaces as the trill [r]: word-finally (⟨eder⟩ [eder], ⟨gaur⟩ [ɡau̯r]) and before a consonant (⟨bernart⟩ [bernart], ⟨korpus⟩ [korpus̺]); ⟨rr⟩ is always the trill (Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003). The falling diphthongs ⟨ai ei oi au eu⟩ are tautosyllabic with a non-syllabic offglide [i̯ u̯]. Coda /n/ before a labial /b p m/ assimilates in place to [m] (⟨anbulantzia⟩ [ambulants̻ia]; Hualde, Lujanbio & Zubiri 2010: 120). STRESS: Basque accent varies by dialect and the Batua spelling never marks it; the stress block states the General Central [+2] pattern (accent on the second syllable) that Batua speech uses (Hualde 1994: 1559; Elordieta, Gaminde & Hualde 1998: 402), and its notes name the dialects that differ. Palatalization of n/l after i (mina [miɲa], mutila [mutiʎa]) is LEXICALLY CONDITIONED in Batua, not automatic phonology — Latinate loans (familia, filosofia, kilometro, kilo) keep plain n/l for educated speakers (Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003, §2.3 notes the variability) — so it is deliberately NOT an allophone rule; downstream lexicons own it.

stress.notes: Batua has no official accent norm. The spelling marks no accent, and the pattern that standard speech uses is the General Central [+2]: the accent falls on the second syllable of the word, counted from the left. Hualde (1994: 1559) proposes it for Batua (mendía, txakúrra, emákumea, bertsólariarekin). Elordieta, Gaminde & Hualde (1998: 399-400) report it as the pattern that spreads through Batua, and their summary of young Donostia Batua speakers (1998: 402) puts every word of three or more syllables on [+2] (gizóna, autóbusa, txistúlaria, basérritarrarentzat). The Euskaltzaindia handbook (Euskara Batuaren Eskuliburua, 'azentua') describes the same [+2] prominence. A disyllable takes the accent on its second syllable (gizón, atál, enbór; Elordieta et al. 1998: 402); in the same speakers a disyllable that ends in a vowel takes it on the first (áte, méndi), but listeners reject that pattern (1998: 403), and the spec keeps [+2]. Not modelled, because the spelling does not show them: a monosyllabic root takes the accent on its first syllable (lúrra, lúrrari, béltzari; Hualde 1994: 1559; Elordieta et al. 1998: 402), and so does a closed set of marked words (lékuan, bésteari, áurrera, átzetik; Hualde 1994: 1559). The weak secondary accent on the last syllable of a phrase (Hualde 1994: 1559, rule III) is a phrase-level fact and is not written. The vowel sequences ⟨ia ea oa ua⟩ are hiatus (Hualde 1994: 1549, [a.te.a], [ba.so.a]); only the falling diphthongs ⟨ai ei oi ui au eu⟩ are one nucleus. onset_clusters is the obstruent + liquid set that Batua spelling opens words with (tren, prest, klase, plaza, flota); an /s/ + stop sequence is not an onset (eus.ka.ra). The dialects differ (Hualde 2022: 83-84, 92, 97): the Western (Bizkaian coastal) systems leave most words unaccented and place the accent at phrase level; Antzuola-Bergara has [-2], Azpeitia-Azkoitia [+3], Hondarribia a quantity-sensitive [-1]/[-2] of the stem, and Goizueta-Oiartzun a high/low tonal contrast on [+1] or [+2]; east of the Bidasoa, including Zuberoan, Roncalese, Lapurdian and Lower Navarrese, the accent is penultimate [-2]. The Eastern dialect specs declare their own penultimate block. Known engine limit: the mark is written inside the affricates ts̻ ts̺ (beltˈs̻aɾi instead of belˈts̻aɾi), because the IPA segmenter does not read an affricate with a diacritic below as one segment.

ancestors.notes: Latin/Romance adstrate: two millennia of contact left a very large lexical layer.
Spanish adstrate: modern loanwords and phonological pressure.
French adstrate: on the northern (Iparralde) dialects.

allophone_rules.notes: Nasal place assimilation (Hualde, Lujanbio & Zubiri 2010:120): coda /n/ before a labial /b p m/ surfaces as [m], e.g. anbulantzia [ambulants̩ia], denbora [dembora].
Intervocalic spirantization (Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003, §2.2.2: voiced stops surface as approximants/fricatives after a vowel, as in Spanish): egin [eɣin], abere [aβeɾe], adar [aðar].
Intervocalic spirantization (Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003, §2.2.2: voiced stops surface as approximants/fricatives after a vowel, as in Spanish): egin [eɣin], abere [aβeɾe], adar [aðar].
Intervocalic spirantization (Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003, §2.2.2: voiced stops surface as approximants/fricatives after a vowel, as in Spanish): egin [eɣin], abere [aβeɾe], adar [aðar].
Closing diphthongs (Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003, §2.4): postvocalic high vowel not followed by a vowel is an offglide — ai [aj], au [aw], gau [ɡaw], sei [sej].
Closing diphthongs (Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003, §2.4): postvocalic high vowel not followed by a vowel is an offglide — ai [aj], au [aw], gau [ɡaw], sei [sej].
